b: Strange, vivid and uncompromising. Ezekiel prophesies to the exiles in Babylon, with dramatised sign-acts and extended visions. The valley of dry bones in chapter 37 is the best known.
Chapter 34 — God against Israel's shepherds, promising to shepherd the flock himself — stands directly behind Jesus' shepherd language.

1.t: Wheels within wheels, and at the end the likeness of a throne and a figure on it. Ezekiel's careful hedging language — likeness, appearance — is the point.
Ezekiel piles up qualifiers because he is describing something he cannot describe. Then he falls face down.

34.t: God condemns Israel's leaders for feeding themselves and says he will search for his sheep himself. Jesus' 'I am the good shepherd' is spoken against this background.
My servant David. Ezekiel's promise is the background to John 10.

36.t: I will show the holiness of my great name. The clearest statement in the prophets of why God restores.
Clean water, a heart of flesh for one of stone, and God's Spirit put within. The mechanics of the new covenant.

37.t: Can these bones live? Ezekiel's answer — O Lord GOD, you know — is the only honest one available to him.
The divided kingdom made one under one shepherd. The promise runs past anything the return from exile delivered.

18.t: Against the proverb about fathers eating sour grapes. Personal responsibility stated at length, ending with God taking no pleasure in the death of anyone.

33.t: If he does not warn, the blood is on him. It is the passage behind most of what the New Testament says about speaking up.

2.h: Whether they listen or fail to listen
2.t: Said four times. Faithfulness is defined by speaking rather than by results.

3.t: Sweet as honey in his mouth. John does the same thing in Revelation 10.

11.t: I will remove from them their heart of stone. Repeated more fully at 36:26.

16.t: Jerusalem as an abandoned infant, rescued, adorned and then unfaithful. It ends with God establishing his covenant anyway.

22.h: I looked for someone to stand in the gap
22.t: And found no one. One of the starkest verses on intercession in Scripture.

47.t: Ankle deep, knee deep, waist deep, then too deep to cross. Revelation 22 picks it up.

4.t: 390 days on one side and 40 on the other, cooking over dung. Prophecy performed with the prophet's own body.

8.h: What they do in the dark
8.t: Ezekiel is shown elders burning incense to idols in a hidden room, saying the LORD does not see us.

10.t: It moves from the threshold, then to the east gate, then away. The temple's destruction follows because God has already left.

12.t: Ezekiel packs his bags in daylight and leaves through a hole at dusk, as a sign of the coming exile.

14.t: Could save only themselves. Righteousness is not transferable, which is what makes the cross necessary.

20.h: For the sake of my name
20.t: Repeated through a long retelling of Israel's rebellion. God's reason for acting is his own character, not their merit.

24.t: Ezekiel is told not to mourn publicly, as a sign to the people. The cost of being a sign is real.

28.t: A lament using Eden imagery. Many read it as also describing a fall behind the human king; the text's primary subject is the king.

39.h: I will pour out my Spirit
39.t: On the house of Israel. The same promise as Joel, in a different register.

43.t: From the east, the way it left in chapter 10. The structure of the book turns on those two movements.

5.t: The hair divided into thirds: burned, struck, scattered. A drama of what is coming to Jerusalem.

6.t: Those who escape will remember me and loathe themselves. Repentance growing out of judgement.

7.t: Repeated like a drumbeat. Ezekiel's most concentrated judgement oracle.

9.h: A mark on those who grieve
9.t: Those who sigh over the city's sins are marked and spared. Revelation 7 echoes it.

13.t: False prophets cover over danger with 'peace'. God will bring the wall down on them.

15.t: Vine wood is good for nothing but burning, and even less after it has been burned.

17.t: God plants a cedar on a high mountain, and birds of every kind nest in it. Jesus' mustard seed parable draws on the image.

19.t: Judah's kings pictured as lions caught in nets.

21.h: Until he comes to whom it rightfully belongs
21.t: The crown removed from Zedekiah until a rightful king arrives. Read messianically from early on.

23.t: Two sisters representing Samaria and Jerusalem, in deliberately shocking sexual imagery about idolatry. It is meant to offend. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

25.t: Ammon, Moab, Edom and Philistia judged for gloating over Judah's fall.

26.t: A bare rock for spreading nets. Conservative interpreters see it fulfilled in stages, with Alexander's destruction of the island city in 332 BC; others note Tyre was later rebuilt and read the oracle more generally. Either way, the great trading power of Ezekiel's day did not survive.

27.t: A lament picturing the city as a great merchant vessel that sinks. Revelation 18 borrows its cargo list.

29.t: The great monster in the Nile, claiming the river as his own creation.

30.t: Egypt's allies fall with her. Judah had repeatedly looked to Egypt for protection against Babylon, and Ezekiel's point is that the power they trusted instead of God cannot even save itself.

31.t: Assyria as a great tree brought down, a warning to Egypt.

32.t: Egypt joins the uncircumcised in the pit. A grim tour of fallen empires.

35.t: Edom judged for its ancient hostility and for rejoicing at Israel's ruin.

38.t: An end-times invasion defeated by God. Interpretations range from a specific future war to a symbolic picture of the final assault on God's people. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

40.t: Nine chapters of measurements. Readers divide on whether this describes a literal future temple, the church, or the new creation; Revelation 21 draws on it for the new Jerusalem. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

41.t: Measured precisely. Detail as an expression of holiness.

42.h: Separating the holy from the common
42.t: The purpose of the wall around the temple area.

44.t: The gate the glory entered is shut, because the LORD has come through it.

45.t: Rulers told to use honest weights and measures. The vision of worship includes economic justice.

46.t: Those who enter by the north go out by the south. No one leaves the way they came.

48.t: The last words of the book and the new name of the city. Everything Ezekiel saw leave returns.
